Unclaimed documents: if you choose office pickup, I hold your documents for up to 30 calendar days after I let you know they are ready. If they remain unclaimed after 30 days without prior arrangement, they will be returned to you at your expense via trackable carrier or securely shredded in accordance with document retention guidelines.

Your receipt, line by line: everything I charge in the apostille process gets its own line, from the notarization to the final delivery:

  • Notarization: $15 per notarial act (Colorado maximum), always on its own line. For Full-Service, it is itemized within the $150 base rate.
  • Apostille / courier service: the rest of the base rate for the option you chose.
  • Travel or mileage: only if it applies.
  • Colorado State fees: $15 same-day or $5 standard per document, at cost.
  • Return: the option you chose with standard processing ($45, $35 office pickup, $5 + label at cost, or $0).

One thing to know: how long the Secretary of State takes depends entirely on their office and their workload. I can’t control or promise the exact day a document comes back.

Courier terms (also on your invoice):

  • Paid for the run, not the result: the courier fee covers pickup, travel, parking, counter time, and delivery, and is earned once the documents are submitted to the Secretary of State.
  • Rejected documents: if the State rejects a document because of how it was prepared or notarized (for example an expired commission, a missing seal, or an incomplete certificate), the courier fee is still owed, any State fee the State keeps is your cost, and a corrected resubmission is a new run at normal rates.
  • Courtesy check only: my look at seals, dates, and certificates is a courtesy, not a legal review. Making sure the documents comply is up to the client and the notary who prepared them.
  • State fees: the State takes only cash, check, or money order, so they’re paid upfront or at pickup.
  • Liability: limited to the fees paid on the order, except for documents lost or damaged through my own negligence.
3

Before you send it: checklist

Most rejections at the Secretary of State come from small notary mistakes: a missing county, a missing date, or an incomplete stamp. Check your documents against this list before you mail or drop them off.

What the Colorado Secretary of State looks for

✔The notary certificate must show:

  • The state and county where it was notarized (e.g., "State of Colorado, County of Douglas").
  • The exact date of notarization, not pre- or post-dated.
  • The correct wording for the act: acknowledgment or jurat (oath).
  • The notary's signature, matching the one on file with the Secretary of State.
  • A clear, complete stamp: notary's name, "Notary Public," "State of Colorado," notary ID number and commission expiration date.
  • A commission that was active on the date of notarization.

✔The document must:

  • Be the original with an ink signature, not a photocopy or scan.
  • Have no blank spaces left unfilled.
  • Be notarized by a Colorado notary (documents notarized in another state are authenticated in that state).
  • For birth, marriage or death records: be a certified copy from the issuing office. A notary cannot certify copies of public records (what a notary can certify).
  • Not ask the notary to certify that someone is alive, or include legal statements the notary isn't allowed to make.

I check every document against this list before I go to the Secretary of State. If something’s missing, I’ll tell you first so it can be fixed. Source: Colorado Secretary of State.

Apostille FAQ

Yes. The Local Denver Courier and Statewide Expedited Courier are only for documents that are already notarized by a Colorado notary. I do not notarize documents that arrive by mail. If you still need the notarization, choose the Full-Service Apostille (local only).

Almost always because of small notary mistakes: a missing county, a missing date, an incomplete or blurry stamp, wrong certificate wording, or blank spaces left in the document. They also reject copies a notary is not allowed to certify, such as birth certificates. Check the requirements list before you send anything.

Full-Service is local only: the Denver Metro area. Outside this area I can travel if the mileage fee is paid. If you live far away, the easiest option is to have your documents notarized by a Colorado notary near you and use the Statewide Expedited Courier.

No. The Colorado Secretary of State only authenticates signatures of Colorado notaries and officials. A document notarized in another state must go to that state's Secretary of State. Federal documents (for example, FBI background checks) are authenticated by the U.S. Department of State.
